claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signal through allostery.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signal through allostery, and it is increasingly clear that chemically distinct agonists can produce different receptor-based effects.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Chemically distinct agonists can produce different receptor-based effects.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signal through allostery, and it is increasingly clear that chemically distinct agonists can produce different receptor-based effects.
evidence: This is presented as an increasingly clear observation in the field.

claim: Different agonists drive GPCRs to engage different cytoplasmic proteins in living cells.
source: However, the underlying hypothesis - that different agonists drive GPCRs to engage different cytoplasmic proteins in living cells - remains untested due to the complexity of readouts through which receptor-proximal interactions are typically inferred.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data demonstrating differential recruitment of biosensors and GRK2 by different agonists.

claim: GPCR-interacting biosensors can be disconnected from endogenous transduction mechanisms.
source: We describe a cell-based assay to overcome this challenge, based on GPCR-interacting biosensors that are disconnected from endogenous transduction mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of engineered proteins (Nb33 and mGsi) that bind activated receptors but are not known to engage other cellular proteins.

claim: Chemically distinct opioid ligands produce differences in biosensor recruitment in living cells.
source: Focusing on opioid receptors, we directly demonstrate differences between biosensor recruitment produced by chemically distinct opioid ligands in living cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents TIR-FM data showing differential recruitment of mGsi and Nb33 by various opioid agonists.

claim: Selective recruitment applies to GRK2 through discrete interactions with receptors or with G protein beta-gamma subunits which are differentially promoted by agonists.
source: We then show that selective recruitment applies to GRK2, a biologically relevant GPCR regulator, through discrete interactions of GRK2 with receptors or with G protein beta-gamma subunits which are differentially promoted by agonists.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that DynA promotes both modes of GRK2 recruitment while ET only promotes recruitment via G beta-gamma.

claim: GPCRs are conformationally flexible.
source: Over the past decade an expanded view has taken hold, supported by accumulating in vitro evidence that GPCRs are conformationally flexible (Lohse and Hofmann, 2015; Mahoney and Sunahara, 2016; Nygaard et al., 2013; Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Wingler et al., 2019) and a confluence of cell biological and in vivo evidence supporting the existence of functionally selective agonist effects (Smith et al., 2018; Urban et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Functionally selective agonist effects exist.
source: Over the past decade an expanded view has taken hold, supported by accumulating in vitro evidence that GPCRs are conformationally flexible (Lohse and Hofmann, 2015; Mahoney and Sunahara, 2016; Nygaard et al., 2013; Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Wingler et al., 2019) and a confluence of cell biological and in vivo evidence supporting the existence of functionally selective agonist effects (Smith et al., 2018; Urban et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cell biological and in vivo studies.

claim: Agonists have the potential to promote GPCRs to selectively recruit one transducer or regulator protein over another.
source: According to this still-evolving view, agonists have the potential to promote GPCRs to selectively recruit one transducer or regulator protein over another, introducing bias into the signaling cascade at a receptor-proximal level that is either propagated downstream or eliminated during intermediate transduction steps (Lau et al., 2011; Tsvetanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is presented as a theoretical view supported by citations and is experimentally tested in this manuscript.

claim: Opioid receptors can be activated by diverse peptide and non-peptide agonists.
source: Interest in selective agonist effects at these GPCRs dates back to the initial demonstration that opioid receptors can be activated by diverse peptide and non-peptide agonists (Kosterlitz and Hughes, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to early work on opioid receptors.

claim: An agonist-induced state of opioid receptors in neuroblastoma cells discriminates between opioid peptides and opiate alkaloids.
source: Early experimental evidence for such selectivity among ligands emerged from the observation of an agonist-induced state of opioid receptors in neuroblastoma cells that discriminates between opioid peptides and opiate alkaloids (Von Zastrow et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Agonist-selective control of opioid receptor endocytosis has been demonstrated.
source: This was followed by the demonstration of agonist-selective control of opioid receptor endocytosis, leading to the identification of functional selectivity among agonists defined by differences in relative ability to drive receptor engagement of G protein relative to beta-arrestin-dependent cellular pathways (Keith et al., 1998; Keith et al., 1996; Whistler et al., 1999; Whistler and von Zastrow, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Selective protein recruitment by GPCRs in intact cells remains largely calculated rather than directly observed.
source: First, selective protein recruitment by GPCRs in intact cells remains largely calculated rather than directly observed.
evidence: This is presented as a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The understanding of receptor-proximal agonist bias is inherently limited by assumptions of the model used to calculate it.
source: Accordingly, the understanding of receptor-proximal agonist bias is inherently limited by assumptions of the model used to calculate it (Kenakin, 2018; Klein Herenbrink et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing limitations of operational models.

claim: Significant challenges remain in reliably assessing selectivity of receptor-proximal protein recruitment based on downstream cell-based readouts.
source: Indeed, and despite intense efforts motivated by interest in the therapeutic impact of biased agonist effects at opioid receptors (Johnson et al., 2017; Schmid et al., 2017; Whistler et al., 1999), significant challenges remain in reliably assessing selectivity of receptor-proximal protein recruitment based on downstream cell-based readouts (Conibear and Kelly, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation discussing challenges in the field.

claim: Beta-arrestin binding to GPCRs involves multiple biochemical steps.
source: For example, multiple methods have been developed to detect GPCR interaction with beta-arrestins in intact cells (Chen et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017). However, this binding involves multiple biochemical steps and, in particular, it typically requires the receptor to undergo prior agonist-induced phosphorylation (Eichel et al., 2018; Gurevich et al., 1995; Thomsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on beta-arrestin recruitment.

claim: Beta-arrestin binding to GPCRs typically requires the receptor to undergo prior agonist-induced phosphorylation.
source: However, this binding involves multiple biochemical steps and, in particular, it typically requires the receptor to undergo prior agonist-induced phosphorylation (Eichel et al., 2018; Gurevich et al., 1995; Thomsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on GPCR phosphorylation and beta-arrestin recruitment.

claim: Full interaction of opioid receptors with beta-arrestin requires the receptor to be phosphorylated at multiple sites in the cytoplasmic tail.
source: This has been clearly established for opioid receptors (Whistler and von Zastrow, 1998; Zhang et al., 1998), for which full interaction with beta-arrestin requires the receptor to be phosphorylated at multiple sites in the cytoplasmic tail through a defined sequence of agonist-dependent reactions which are catalyzed by distinct GPCR kinase (GRK) isoforms (Chiu et al., 2017; Just et al., 2013; Lau et al., 2011; Miess et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on opioid receptor phosphorylation.

claim: Opioid receptor phosphorylation occurs through a defined sequence of agonist-dependent reactions catalyzed by distinct GRK isoforms.
source: This has been clearly established for opioid receptors (Whistler and von Zastrow, 1998; Zhang et al., 1998), for which full interaction with beta-arrestin requires the receptor to be phosphorylated at multiple sites in the cytoplasmic tail through a defined sequence of agonist-dependent reactions which are catalyzed by distinct GPCR kinase (GRK) isoforms (Chiu et al., 2017; Just et al., 2013; Lau et al., 2011; Miess et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on GRK-mediated phosphorylation.

claim: Two agonist-activated opioid receptor complexes have been described in structural detail: one bound to a nucleotide-free G protein heterotrimer and another to an active state-stabilizing nanobody.
source: Two agonist-activated opioid receptor complexes have been described in structural detail (Figure 1A), one bound to a nucleotide-free G protein heterotrimer and another to an active state-stabilizing nanobody (Nb) (Huang et al., 2015; Koehl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and Figure 1A shows the structures.

claim: The receptor conformation in the G protein-bound complex is similar but not identical to the nanobody-bound complex.
source: The receptor conformation resolved in each complex is similar but not identical, with Nb and G protein interactions involving distinct molecular contacts on cytoplasmic domains of the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nb and G protein interactions involve distinct molecular contacts on cytoplasmic domains of the receptor.
source: The receptor conformation resolved in each complex is similar but not identical, with Nb and G protein interactions involving distinct molecular contacts on cytoplasmic domains of the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nanobodies are inherently orthogonal to intracellular biochemistry.
source: Nbs are inherently orthogonal to intracellular biochemistry but heterotrimeric G proteins engage multiple cellular proteins in addition to activated receptors.
evidence: This is stated as a property of nanobodies based on their nature as engineered proteins.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins engage multiple cellular proteins in addition to activated receptors.
source: Nbs are inherently orthogonal to intracellular biochemistry but heterotrimeric G proteins engage multiple cellular proteins in addition to activated receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about G protein signaling.

claim: Mini-G proteins are engineered versions of the Ras-like domain of G protein alpha subunits which bind directly to activated GPCRs but are not known to engage other cellular proteins.
source: Thus we focused on mini-G (mG) proteins, engineered versions of the Ras-like domain of G protein alpha subunits which bind directly to activated GPCRs but are not known to engage other cellular proteins (Nehmé et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies describing mini-G proteins.

claim: mGsi is derived from the Ras-like domain of Gs alpha with nine residues at the distal C-terminus replaced by corresponding residues from Gi alpha1.
source: For a mG probe we chose mGsi, derived from the Ras-like domain of Gs alpha but with nine residues at the distal C-terminus replaced by the corresponding residues from Gi alpha1.
evidence: This describes the design of the mGsi probe used in the study.

claim: The C-terminal residues of G protein alpha subunits form a major determinant of G protein coupling specificity.
source: These C-terminal residues form a major determinant of G protein coupling specificity (Conklin et al., 1993) by folding into a helical structure (alpha-5 helix) that occupies the agonist-activated GPCR core (Carpenter and Tate, 2017; Koehl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on G protein coupling.

claim: The C-terminal residues of G protein alpha subunits fold into a helical structure (alpha-5 helix) that occupies the agonist-activated GPCR core.
source: These C-terminal residues form a major determinant of G protein coupling specificity (Conklin et al., 1993) by folding into a helical structure (alpha-5 helix) that occupies the agonist-activated GPCR core (Carpenter and Tate, 2017; Koehl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Gs couples poorly to opioid receptors.
source: Because Gs couples poorly to opioid receptors, we reasoned that a sensor derived from mGsi would primarily detect this interaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about opioid receptor signaling.

claim: Nb33 was previously used to detect activated mu and delta opioid receptors in living cells.
source: For a Nb probe we selected Nb33, previously used to detect activated mu (MOR) and delta (DOR) opioid receptors in living cells (Stoeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nb33 shares receptor contact residues with Nb39.
source: Nb33 shares receptor contact residues with Nb39, a close analog that has been resolved at high resolution in complex with activated MOR (Huang et al., 2015) and in a similar complex with activated kappa opioid receptor (KOR) (Che et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic residues contacted by Nb39 are largely distinct from those engaged by the G protein alpha-5 helix.
source: Because cytoplasmic residues contacted by the Nb in these structures are largely distinct from those engaged by the G protein alpha-5 helix, we reasoned that the Nb-derived sensor has the potential to provide different allosteric information.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data cited in the manuscript.

claim: HEK293 cells do not express endogenous opioid receptors or other opioid ligand binding sites.
source: Importantly, HEK293 cells do not express endogenous opioid receptors or other opioid ligand binding sites, thereby providing a null genetic background on which to directly examine protein probe recruitment mediated specifically by the co-expressed receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HEK293 cells.

claim: Dynorphin A produces rapid and robust recruitment of mGsi by KOR.
source: We observed rapid and robust recruitment of mGsi by KOR upon application of the kappa-selective peptide agonist Dynorphin A (DynA, Dynorphin 1–17).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Recruitment of mGsi by KOR is reversible upon application of the antagonist 5'GNTI.
source: Recruitment of mGsi was reversible because application of the high-affinity competitive KOR antagonist 5'GNTI resulted in rapid redistribution of the biosensor back to the cytoplasm (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: mGs is not detectably recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA.
source: In contrast, mGs was not detectably recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA using the same assay (Figure 1F), verifying assay specificity and that mGsi recruitment is driven primarily by the Gi-derived distal C-terminus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: mGsi recruitment is driven primarily by the Gi-derived distal C-terminus.
source: In contrast, mGs was not detectably recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA using the same assay (Figure 1F), verifying assay specificity and that mGsi recruitment is driven primarily by the Gi-derived distal C-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of mGs and mGsi recruitment data.

claim: Agonist-induced recruitment of mGsi occurs separately from a change in surface expression of KOR.
source: Further, we verified that agonist-induced recruitment of mGsi occurred separately from a change in surface expression of KOR, which was monitored in parallel using anti-Flag antibody (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by parallel monitoring of KOR surface expression in Figure 1D.

claim: Nb33 is rapidly recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA.
source: Nb33 was also rapidly recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA using the same experimental protocol, and this recruitment was also reversible upon antagonist application and occurred without a detectable change in surface receptor expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nb33 recruitment by KOR is reversible upon antagonist application.
source: Nb33 was also rapidly recruited in response to KOR activation by DynA using the same experimental protocol, and this recruitment was also reversible upon antagonist application and occurred without a detectable change in surface receptor expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both mGsi and Nb33 produce a reversible recruitment signal that is sufficiently robust and fast (t1/2 < 30 s).
source: Accordingly, both mGsi and Nb33 can be used as biosensors of ligand-dependent recruitment by KOR in living cells using the TIR-FM assay, and both sensors produce a reversible recruitment signal that is sufficiently robust and fast (t1/2< 30 s) to enable reliable detection of protein recruitment without possible complications of later receptor trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: U69593 and U50488 are non-peptide KOR full agonists.
source: We next tested two non-peptide KOR full agonists, U69593 (U69) and U50488 (U50).
evidence: This is established pharmacology of these compounds, supported by citation.

claim: Both Nb33 and mGsi are robustly recruited in a concentration-dependent manner in response to DynA, U69, and U50.
source: Both Nb33 and mGsi were robustly recruited in a concentration-dependent manner in response to DynA and both of the non-peptide full agonist drugs (Figure 1I–K), consistent with the previously established pharmacology of these compounds (DiMattio et al., 2015), but we also noted that the concentration-response relationship for mGsi recruitment was consistently left-shifted relative to Nb33.
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response curves in Figures 1I-K.

claim: The concentration-response relationship for mGsi recruitment by KOR is consistently left-shifted relative to Nb33.
source: Both Nb33 and mGsi were robustly recruited in a concentration-dependent manner in response to DynA and both of the non-peptide full agonist drugs (Figure 1I–K), consistent with the previously established pharmacology of these compounds (DiMattio et al., 2015), but we also noted that the concentration-response relationship for mGsi recruitment was consistently left-shifted relative to Nb33.
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response curves in Figures 1I-K.

claim: Etorphine is an opiate alkaloid drug that is structurally distinct from opioid peptides as well as from U50 and U69.
source: ET is an opiate alkaloid drug that is structurally distinct from opioid peptides as well as from U50 and U69.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemical structure of etorphine.

claim: Etorphine efficaciously promotes G protein activation and signaling.
source: ET is an opiate alkaloid drug that is structurally distinct from opioid peptides as well as from U50 and U69. ET efficaciously promotes G protein activation and signaling but has long been recognized to drive KOR internalization and phosphorylation poorly, supporting its classification as a G protein-biased agonist by operational criteria (Chu et al., 1997; DiMattio et al., 2015; Jordan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Etorphine drives KOR internalization and phosphorylation poorly.
source: ET efficaciously promotes G protein activation and signaling but has long been recognized to drive KOR internalization and phosphorylation poorly, supporting its classification as a G protein-biased agonist by operational criteria (Chu et al., 1997; DiMattio et al., 2015; Jordan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Etorphine is classified as a G protein-biased agonist by operational criteria.
source: ET efficaciously promotes G protein activation and signaling but has long been recognized to drive KOR internalization and phosphorylation poorly, supporting its classification as a G protein-biased agonist by operational criteria (Chu et al., 1997; DiMattio et al., 2015; Jordan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Etorphine behaves as a potent but partial agonist in the mGsi recruitment assay, producing a maximum recruitment response reaching 67% of that produced by DynA.
source: ET behaved as a potent but partial agonist in the mGsi recruitment assay, producing a maximum biosensor recruitment response reaching 67% of that produced by DynA (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figures 2A and 2D.

claim: Etorphine produces little or no recruitment of Nb33 by KOR despite a robust response to DynA.
source: Remarkably, ET produced little or no recruitment of Nb33 despite a robust response to DynA verified in each assay and in the same cells (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figures 2B and 2E.

claim: Etorphine fails to recruit Nb33 even at very high concentrations.
source: This lack of Nb33 recruitment was evident even at very high concentrations of ET (Figure 2B and C), in contrast to mGsi that was potently recruited (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Selective recruitment of mGsi relative to Nb33 by etorphine is observed when the biosensors are co-expressed and imaged in parallel in the same cells.
source: Further verifying this difference, selective recruitment of mGsi relative to Nb33 was observed when the biosensors were tagged with distinct fluorophores, co-expressed, and imaged in parallel in the same cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dual-color TIR-FM data in Figure 2F.

claim: mG and Nb probes can distinguish receptor-proximal agonist effects in intact cells.
source: These results indicate that mG and Nb probes can distinguish receptor-proximal agonist effects in intact cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential recruitment data for etorphine vs. DynA.

claim: Agonist-induced internalization of KOR requires multi-site phosphorylation on its cytoplasmic tail.
source: In particular, because agonist-induced internalization of KOR requires multi-site phosphorylation on its cytoplasmic tail, and ET is known to stimulate this phosphorylation less strongly than DynA (Chen et al., 2016), we considered the possibility that differential biosensor recruitment occurs secondarily to differential phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Etorphine stimulates KOR phosphorylation less strongly than DynA.
source: In particular, because agonist-induced internalization of KOR requires multi-site phosphorylation on its cytoplasmic tail, and ET is known to stimulate this phosphorylation less strongly than DynA (Chen et al., 2016), we considered the possibility that differential biosensor recruitment occurs secondarily to differential phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pronounced difference in mGsi relative to Nb33 recruitment by etorphine is still observed using KOR-TPD (a mutant lacking all relevant phosphorylation sites).
source: To test this, we measured biosensor recruitment by a mutant KOR lacking all relevant phosphorylation sites in the cytoplasmic tail (KOR-TPD for 'total phosphorylation defective', Figure 2H). The pronounced difference in mGsi relative to Nb33 recruitment was still observed (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: Selective probe recruitment by wild type KOR is not detectably perturbed in the presence of Compound101, a GRK2/3 inhibitor.
source: Independently verifying this, selective probe recruitment by wild type KOR was not detectably perturbed in the presence of Compound101 (Figure 2K), a chemical inhibitor of GRK2/3 activity known to strongly reduce KOR phosphorylation in HEK293 cells (Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2K.

claim: Selective recruitment of mG relative to Nb probes occurs as a primary consequence of allosteric protein selection at the receptor, rather than a secondary effect of differential phosphorylation.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that selective recruitment of mG relative to Nb probes occurs as a primary consequence of allosteric protein selection at the receptor, rather than a secondary effect of differential phosphorylation.
evidence: This is concluded from the KOR-TPD and Compound101 experiments.

claim: Nb33 is recruited by agonist-activated MORs.
source: Nb33 is already known to be recruited by agonist-activated MORs (Stoeber et al., 2018), and we verified that this is also the case for mGsi.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and verified by data in the current study.

claim: DAMGO produces rapid and robust recruitment of mGsi by MOR that is rapidly reversed by naloxone.
source: DAMGO, a peptide full agonist of MOR, produced rapid and robust recruitment of mGsi that was rapidly reversed by the competitive antagonist naloxone (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The concentration-response relationship for recruitment of mGsi by DAMGO is left-shifted relative to Nb33.
source: Similar to what was observed for recruitment of the engineered protein probes by KOR, the concentration-response relationship for recruitment of mGsi by DAMGO was left-shifted relative to Nb33 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: Etorphine promotes recruitment of both mGsi and Nb33 by MOR to the same maximum degree as DAMGO.
source: ET (also an agonist of MOR) promoted recruitment of both probes by MOR, and to the same maximum degree when compared to the peptide full agonist (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figure 3C.

claim: Differential recruitment of engineered protein probes by opioid receptors is both agonist-dependent and receptor subtype-specific.
source: This contrasts with partial recruitment of mGsi and no detectable recruitment of Nb33 by KOR (Figure 2), indicating that differential recruitment of the engineered protein probes by opioid receptors is both agonist-dependent and receptor subtype-specific.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing etorphine effects on KOR vs. MOR.

claim: Morphine and PZM21 are partial agonists with respect to assays of G protein activation or signaling.
source: Both of these non-peptide drugs are partial agonists with respect to assays of G protein activation or signaling, but each is derived from a different chemical scaffold and differs in degree of bias estimated using a beta-arrestin recruitment assay (Manglik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Morphine and PZM21 differ in degree of bias estimated using a beta-arrestin recruitment assay.
source: Both of these non-peptide drugs are partial agonists with respect to assays of G protein activation or signaling, but each is derived from a different chemical scaffold and differs in degree of bias estimated using a beta-arrestin recruitment assay (Manglik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both morphine and PZM21 produce partial recruitment of mGsi as well as Nb33 by MOR.
source: Using the same experimental protocol, and comparing recruitment promoted by the test ligand relative to the peptide full agonist (DAMGO) reference, both morphine and PZM21 produced partial recruitment of mGsi as well as Nb33 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Morphine and PZM21 are similar in the degree of mGsi recruitment that they produce at saturating concentration.
source: Whereas morphine and PZM21 were similar in the degree of mGsi recruitment that they produced at saturating concentration, morphine was found to be significantly more efficacious than PZM21 in recruiting Nb33.
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figure 3E.

claim: Morphine is significantly more efficacious than PZM21 in recruiting Nb33 to MOR.
source: Whereas morphine and PZM21 were similar in the degree of mGsi recruitment that they produced at saturating concentration, morphine was found to be significantly more efficacious than PZM21 in recruiting Nb33.
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a range of selective protein recruitment effects among chemically diverse MOR partial agonists.
source: Together, these results reveal a range of selective protein recruitment effects among chemically diverse MOR partial agonists.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential recruitment data for morphine and PZM21.

claim: Mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP) is a semi-synthetic natural product and MOR partial agonist.
source: We found evidence for this when evaluating another chemically distinct MOR partial agonist, the semi-synthetic natural product mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP) (Váradi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MP promotes mGsi recruitment by MOR to a significantly reduced maximal degree relative to DAMGO.
source: With this modification, MP was verified to indeed promote mGsi recruitment by MOR, but to a significantly reduced maximal degree relative to DAMGO and without promoting detectable recruitment of Nb33 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: MP does not promote detectable recruitment of Nb33 to MOR.
source: With this modification, MP was verified to indeed promote mGsi recruitment by MOR, but to a significantly reduced maximal degree relative to DAMGO and without promoting detectable recruitment of Nb33 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-response data in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: The ability to promote selective protein recruitment is widespread among chemically diverse opioid agonists.
source: They further suggest that the ability to promote selective protein recruitment is widespread among chemically diverse opioid agonists (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of multiple agonists shown in Figure 4.

claim: Some non-peptide agonists recruit both protein probes to a similar maximal degree as the reference peptide.
source: Some non-peptide agonists were indistinguishable from the reference peptide by this analysis, recruiting both protein probes to a similar maximal degree (corresponding to an 'I.A.' value of 1 for both probes), but others departed from the diagonal.
evidence: This is shown in the plot in Figure 4B.

claim: The observed selectivity of protein recruitment is not consistent with the traditional concept of partial agonism based on a unitary agonist-induced receptor 'on' state.
source: This is not consistent with the traditional concept of partial agonism based on a unitary agonist-induced receptor 'on' state, which would predict the recruitment responses elicited by all agonists to fall along the diagonal.
evidence: This is inferred from the deviation of data points from the diagonal in Figure 4B.

claim: Opioid receptors are flexibly activated, enabling them to selectively recruit one interaction probe over another in living cells.
source: Rather, the present results support the view that opioid receptors are more flexibly activated, enabling them to selectively recruit one interaction probe over another in living cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential recruitment data across multiple agonists.

claim: GRK2 is important for generating agonist-selective patterns of multi-site phosphorylation in the MOR cytoplasmic tail.
source: We focused on GRK2 because this kinase is known to be important for generating agonist-selective patterns of multi-site phosphorylation in the MOR cytoplasmic tail, which convey biased effects downstream from the receptor by distinguishing engagement of beta-arrestins and regulating receptor entry into the endocytic network (Just et al., 2013; Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Agonist-selective patterns of MOR phosphorylation convey biased effects downstream by distinguishing engagement of beta-arrestins and regulating receptor entry into the endocytic network.
source: We focused on GRK2 because this kinase is known to be important for generating agonist-selective patterns of multi-site phosphorylation in the MOR cytoplasmic tail, which convey biased effects downstream from the receptor by distinguishing engagement of beta-arrestins and regulating receptor entry into the endocytic network (Just et al., 2013; Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GRK2 is recruited by activated GPCRs through multiple interactions, including with the activated GPCR and with beta-gamma subunits.
source: We were also intrigued by GRK2 because it is recruited by activated GPCRs through multiple interactions, including with the activated GPCR and with beta-gamma subunits that are exposed on the inner membrane leaflet following activation of the G protein heterotrimer (DebBurman et al., 1995; Lodowski et al., 2003; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: DynA promotes rapid, concentration-dependent recruitment of GRK2 to the plasma membrane.
source: DynA promoted rapid, concentration-dependent recruitment of GRK2 to the plasma membrane (Figure 5B) while ET, despite being highly potent, produced a degree of GRK2 recruitment clearly lower than that produced by DynA (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figure 5B.

claim: Etorphine produces a degree of GRK2 recruitment clearly lower than that produced by DynA.
source: DynA promoted rapid, concentration-dependent recruitment of GRK2 to the plasma membrane (Figure 5B) while ET, despite being highly potent, produced a degree of GRK2 recruitment clearly lower than that produced by DynA (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The difference in GRK2 recruitment between etorphine and DynA is not a secondary effect of receptor phosphorylation.
source: This difference was not a secondary effect of receptor phosphorylation because ET also produced less maximal GRK2 recruitment than DynA using the phosphorylation-defective mutant KOR-TPD in place of KOR (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 5E and 5F using KOR-TPD.

claim: Etorphine and DynA produce similarly strong recruitment of the isolated C-terminal PH domain from GRK2 that interacts with G beta-gamma.
source: Although ET promoted recruitment of full-length GRK2 less strongly than DynA, these agonists produced similarly strong recruitment of a probe corresponding to the isolated C-terminal PH domain from GRK2 that interacts with G beta-gamma (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figure 5G.

claim: GRK2 binding to G beta-gamma subunits, enabled by G protein activation, is responsible for partial recruitment promoted by etorphine.
source: This suggested that GRK2 binding to G beta-gamma subunits, enabled by G protein activation triggered by either agonist, is responsible for partial recruitment promoted by ET.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRK2 C-tail recruitment data in Figure 5G.

claim: Etorphine fails to produce detectable recruitment of GRK2 in cells pre-exposed to pertussis toxin.
source: We independently verified this conclusion by returning to assay of full length tagged GRK2, and testing the effect of blocking Gi activation by pre-exposing cells to pertussis toxin (PTX). In this condition, ET failed to produce any detectable recruitment of GRK2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figure 5H.

claim: DynA still produces a significant GRK2 recruitment response in cells pre-exposed to pertussis toxin, but to a reduced degree relative to cells not exposed to pertussis toxin.
source: However, as expected, DynA still produced a significant recruitment response in the same cells (Figure 5H), but to a reduced degree relative to the recruitment response elicited by DynA in cells not previously exposed to pertussis toxin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM data in Figure 5H.

claim: Etorphine and DynA share the ability to promote GRK2 recruitment to the plasma membrane via binding G beta-gamma.
source: The above results indicate that ET and DynA share the ability to promote GRK2 recruitment to the plasma membrane via binding G beta-gamma, and that DynA engages an additional mode of binding that is separate from the G protein and not shared with ET.
evidence: This is concluded from the GRK2 C-tail and PTX experiments.

claim: DynA engages an additional mode of GRK2 binding that is separate from the G protein and not shared with etorphine.
source: The above results indicate that ET and DynA share the ability to promote GRK2 recruitment to the plasma membrane via binding G beta-gamma, and that DynA engages an additional mode of binding that is separate from the G protein and not shared with ET.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential GRK2 recruitment data.

claim: DynA specifically promotes accumulation of GRK2 at KOR-containing clusters.
source: Within ~1 min after application of DynA, GRK2 specifically accumulated at the KOR-containing clusters (Figure 6B right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM images in Figure 6B.

claim: Etorphine produces a diffuse increase in GRK2 fluorescence at the plasma membrane but no specific accumulation at KOR-containing clusters.
source: In contrast, application of ET produced a diffuse increase in GRK2 fluorescence at the plasma membrane but no specific accumulation at KOR-containing clusters (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIR-FM images in Figure 6C.

claim: DynA promotes significant accumulation of GRK2 with receptors but etorphine does not.
source: Quantification of the GRK2 intensity in KOR clusters relative to the surrounding plasma membrane verified significant accumulation of GRK2 with receptors promoted by DynA but not ET (Figure 6D), despite both agonists promoting diffuse membrane recruitment (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 6D.

claim: GRK2 engagement is driven by discrete biochemical modes which are differentially regulated by agonists: DynA and ET share the ability to promote GRK2 recruitment via receptor-activated G beta-gamma, but DynA additionally promotes GRK2 recruitment by binding directly to KOR.
source: These results support a model of GRK2 engagement driven by discrete biochemical modes which are differentially regulated by agonists: DynA and ET share the ability to promote GRK2 recruitment to the plasma membrane via receptor-activated G beta-gamma, but DynA is different from ET in its ability to additionally promote GRK2 recruitment by binding directly to KOR (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is the model concluded from all GRK2 recruitment experiments and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Agonists differ in relative ability to drive recruitment of engineered probes to opioid receptors in living cells.
source: We show that agonists differ in relative ability to drive recruitment of the engineered probes to opioid receptors in living cells, and then delineate how the principle of agonist-selective recruitment applies to GRK2 as a physiologically relevant regulator.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, demonstrated by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Selective recruitment of one cellular protein over another occurs in intact cells.
source: Our results indicate that selective recruitment of one cellular protein over another not only occurs in intact cells, but it is widespread and elicited by diverse agonists.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of multiple agonists and probes.

claim: All partial agonists examined promote mGsi recruitment more strongly than Nb33 when present at saturating concentration.
source: All partial agonists examined were found to promote mGsi recruitment more strongly than Nb33 when present at saturating concentration.
evidence: This is shown in the summary data in Figure 4.

claim: Concentration-response curves for mGsi relative to Nb33 recruitment by opioid receptors are left-shifted even for peptide full agonists.
source: Further, concentration-response curves for mGsi relative to Nb33 recruitment by opioid receptors were left-shifted even for peptide full agonists.
evidence: This is shown in the concentration-response data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The present results provide clear biochemical evidence for discrete protein-engaged receptor states that can be selectively produced by diverse agonists in intact, living cells.
source: The present results are fully consistent with this concept, and expand it by providing clear biochemical evidence for discrete protein-engaged receptor states that can be selectively produced by diverse agonists in the complex environment of intact, living cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential recruitment data across multiple agonists and probes.

claim: The engineered interaction probes demonstrate an additional level of allosteric selection most simply.
source: The engineered interaction probes that we focused on here demonstrate such an additional level of allosteric selection most simply, but our results delineating differential recruitment of GRK2 by receptors suggest that the same principle applies in a more complex manner to biologically relevant GPCR-interacting proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the engineered probe data with the GRK2 data.

claim: The same principle of agonist-selective recruitment applies in a more complex manner to biologically relevant GPCR-interacting proteins.
source: The engineered interaction probes that we focused on here demonstrate such an additional level of allosteric selection most simply, but our results delineating differential recruitment of GRK2 by receptors suggest that the same principle applies in a more complex manner to biologically relevant GPCR-interacting proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the GRK2 recruitment data.

claim: It is likely that still more specificity exists in receptor-proximal protein recruitment beyond what was observed with the two probes used.
source: It is possible, and we think likely, that still more specificity exists in receptor-proximal protein recruitment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings with two probes.

claim: The complexes responsible for agonist-selective protein recruitment must be distinct.
source: The present results clearly indicate that the complexes responsible for agonist-selective protein recruitment must be distinct, but leave unresolved the nature of the distinction.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential recruitment data.

claim: Distinct allosteric complexes may reflect unique conformational ensembles of the receptor.
source: One possibility is that distinct allosteric complexes reflect unique conformational ensembles of the receptor.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism for the observed selectivity.

claim: The precise conformation of MOR intracellular loop 3 (ICL3) differs between the Nb39-bound and Gi-bound structures.
source: Both Nb39 and Gi alpha stabilize an active MOR conformation in the intracellular domain; however, the precise conformation of the MOR intracellular loop 3 (ICL3) differs between the two structures.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of published structures.

claim: Differential recruitment of Nb33 and mGsi may reflect agonist-selective stabilization of distinct active receptor conformations.
source: Thus, differential recruitment of Nb33 and mGsi may reflect agonist-selective stabilization of distinct active receptor conformations.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism based on structural data.

claim: Agonists may promote receptors to adopt similar active conformations, and distinctions in the kinetics of sensor binding, sensor concentration, and/or sensor affinity contribute to differential recruitment.
source: Alternatively, agonists may promote receptors to adopt similar active conformations, and distinctions in the kinetics of sensor binding, sensor concentration, and/or sensor affinity contribute to differential recruitment.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative mechanism for the observed selectivity.

claim: The orthogonal probes produce a time-invariant recruitment response within ~30 s after agonist application.
source: We found that the orthogonal probes produce a time-invariant recruitment response within ~30 s after agonist application.
evidence: This is observed from the kinetic data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The approach can be used as an end-point assay scalable to a drug screening platform.
source: This enables the approach to be used as an end-point assay scalable to a drug screening platform, and we focused on steady state recruitment values in the present work for simplicity.
evidence: This is proposed based on the rapid and robust nature of the recruitment response.

claim: GPCRs operate as allosteric machines with the potential to communicate significantly more information about local chemical environment than the mere presence or absence of a cognate agonist.
source: In sum, and viewed more broadly, the present results reinforce an emerging understanding that GPCRs operate as allosteric machines with the potential to communicate significantly more information about local chemical environment than the mere presence or absence of a cognate agonist (Costa-Neto et al., 2016; Kenakin, 2019).
evidence: This is concluded from the findings and supported by citations to related work.

claim: The mGsi probe reports allosteric effects relevant to G protein engagement by opioid receptors.
source: We propose from the present observations that the mGsi probe reports allosteric effects relevant to G protein engagement by opioid receptors, and that the Nb probe reports additional effects relevant to GRK engagement.
evidence: This is proposed based on the differential recruitment patterns observed.

claim: The Nb probe reports additional effects relevant to GRK engagement.
source: We propose from the present observations that the mGsi probe reports allosteric effects relevant to G protein engagement by opioid receptors, and that the Nb probe reports additional effects relevant to GRK engagement.
evidence: This is proposed based on the differential recruitment patterns observed.

claim: Agonist bias can be deconvolved into discrete receptor-proximal molecular selection events.
source: Our results further support the hypothesis that agonist bias, now generally defined by operational criteria, can be deconvolved into discrete receptor-proximal molecular selection events.
evidence: This is concluded from the demonstration of discrete recruitment modes for GRK2.
